learn: Living things share characteristics: they are made of cells, use energy, grow and develop, respond to their environment, reproduce and maintain stable internal conditions.
Keeping internal conditions stable is called homeostasis, like sweating to cool down.
Something must have all the characteristics to be considered alive.
check: All living things are made of...
Fire grows and uses energy. Is it alive?
No, it isn't made of cells
lessons.try: Decide whether fire, a seed and a crystal are alive, using the list.

learn: Living things need energy (food), water, living space and stable conditions.
Producers make their own food; consumers eat other organisms.
Most organisms need oxygen to release energy from food.
check: Organisms that make their own food are...
Most organisms need ___ to release energy.
lessons.try: List what a houseplant and a pet fish each need.

learn: Scientists classify organisms into groups based on shared traits.
Levels go from broad to specific: domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.
Every species has a two-part scientific name, like Homo sapiens for humans.
lessons.try: Make a mnemonic to remember the classification levels.

units.t: Cells: The Basic Unit of Life

learn: Cell theory states: all living things are made of cells, cells are the basic unit of life, and all cells come from existing cells.
Robert Hooke first named cells in 1665 after viewing cork under a microscope.
Anton van Leeuwenhoek was the first to see living single-celled organisms.
check: The basic unit of life is the...
lessons.try: Look at onion skin cells under a microscope or a photograph.

learn: Both have a cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus and mitochondria.
Plant cells also have a cell wall for support and chloroplasts for photosynthesis.
Plant cells often have one large central vacuole.
check: Which do only plant cells have?
lessons.try: Draw and label a plant cell and an animal cell side by side.

learn: The nucleus holds DNA and controls the cell.
Mitochondria release energy from food (the cell's powerhouse). Ribosomes make proteins.
The cell membrane controls what enters and leaves.
check: The "powerhouse" of the cell is the...
The control centre of the cell is the...
lessons.try: Compare a cell to a city: which organelle is the town hall, the power station?

learn: Diffusion is the movement of particles from high concentration to low.
Osmosis is the diffusion of water across a membrane.
These are passive transport: they need no energy.
lessons.try: Put a drop of food colouring in still water and watch it spread.

learn: Active transport moves substances from low to high concentration.
It requires energy from the cell.
Cells use active transport to take in nutrients they need in large amounts.
check: Pushing a cart uphill is like...
lessons.try: Explain active transport using the idea of pushing a cart uphill.

learn: Cells divide so organisms can grow and repair damage.
Mitosis makes two identical cells with the same DNA.
The cell cycle includes growth, copying DNA and dividing.
check: Before dividing, a cell copies its...
lessons.try: Draw the stages of mitosis.

units.t: Levels of Organization and Body Systems

learn: Levels of organization: cells, tissues, organs, organ systems, organism.
A tissue is a group of similar cells. An organ is made of tissues working together.
The heart is an organ made of muscle, nerve and connective tissue.
check: A group of similar cells is a...
lessons.try: Make a diagram from cell to organism for the heart.

learn: The circulatory system (heart, blood, blood vessels) transports oxygen and nutrients.
The respiratory system (lungs, trachea) takes in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide.
These systems work together: blood picks up oxygen in the lungs.
lessons.try: Measure breathing rate and pulse at rest and after exercise.

learn: The digestive system breaks food into nutrients.
The nervous system (brain, spinal cord, nerves) controls the body and processes information.
The skeletal and muscular systems support and move the body.
check: Food is broken down by the...
The brain is part of the...
Bones and muscles work together to...
lessons.try: Trace the path of food through the digestive system.

learn: Plants use sunlight, water and carbon dioxide to make glucose (sugar) and oxygen.
This happens in chloroplasts, which contain green chlorophyll.
Word equation: carbon dioxide + water + light energy → glucose + oxygen.
lessons.try: Place a water plant in sunlight and watch for oxygen bubbles.

learn: Cells release energy from glucose using oxygen.
Word equation: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy.
Respiration happens in mitochondria in both plants and animals.
lessons.try: Compare the two word equations and note how they are opposites.

learn: Photosynthesis and respiration form a cycle.
Plants take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen; animals do the reverse.
This balance helps keep the atmosphere stable.
lessons.try: Draw a diagram of the cycle with a plant and an animal.

learn: Heredity is passing traits from parents to offspring.
Genes are sections of DNA that carry instructions for traits.
Each parent gives one copy of each gene, so offspring get two versions (alleles).
check: Different versions of a gene are...
lessons.try: List inherited traits in your family, like eye colour.

learn: Gregor Mendel studied pea plants in the 1860s and discovered patterns of inheritance.
A dominant allele (T) hides a recessive allele (t).
Tt shows the dominant trait; tt shows the recessive trait.
check: A recessive trait shows only when...
lessons.try: Find which pea traits Mendel studied.

learn: A Punnett square predicts possible offspring.
Tt × Tt gives TT, Tt, Tt, tt: a 3:1 ratio of dominant to recessive.
Probabilities: 75% dominant, 25% recessive.
check: Tt × Tt: chance of tt is...
Tt × tt: chance of Tt is...
lessons.try: Make a Punnett square for Tt × tt.

learn: Individuals in a species vary in their traits.
An adaptation is a trait that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its environment.
Examples: a polar bear's thick fur, a cactus's spines.
check: A trait that helps survival is an...
lessons.try: Describe three adaptations of an animal in a cold climate.

learn: Charles Darwin described natural selection in "On the Origin of Species" (1859).
Organisms with helpful traits survive and reproduce more, passing those traits on.
Over many generations, populations change.
check: Helpful traits become ___ common over time.
lessons.try: Model natural selection with coloured paper "moths" on different backgrounds.

learn: Fossils show how life has changed over time.
Similar bone structures in different animals (like arms, wings and flippers) suggest common ancestry.
DNA comparisons show how closely species are related.
check: Similar bones in different species suggest...
DNA comparisons show how ___ species are.
lessons.try: Compare the bones of a human arm, a bat wing and a whale flipper.

learn: Bacteria are single-celled organisms without a nucleus.
Most bacteria are helpful: they help digest food and recycle nutrients.
Some bacteria cause illnesses; antibiotics can treat bacterial infections.
check: Bacterial infections can be treated with...
lessons.try: List three helpful uses of bacteria.

learn: Viruses are not cells. They need a host cell to make copies of themselves.
Colds and flu are caused by viruses.
Antibiotics do not work on viruses; vaccines help prevent many viral diseases.
check: Antibiotics work on viruses. True or false?
lessons.try: Make a chart comparing bacteria and viruses.

learn: The immune system defends the body against germs.
White blood cells attack invaders and remember them.
Hand washing, sleep and good nutrition support immunity.
lessons.try: Make a poster on preventing the spread of germs.

learn: An ecosystem includes living (biotic) and non-living (abiotic) parts.
Biotic: plants, animals, fungi. Abiotic: sunlight, water, soil, temperature.
A population is one species in an area; a community is all species in an area.
check: All species in an area form a...
lessons.try: List the biotic and abiotic parts of a pond.

learn: Energy flows from producers to consumers to decomposers.
Herbivores eat plants; carnivores eat animals; omnivores eat both.
Food webs show many connected food chains.
check: An animal that eats both plants and animals is an...
lessons.try: Draw a food web for a forest with at least eight organisms.

learn: Only about 10% of energy passes from one level to the next.
The rest is used for life processes or lost as heat.
That is why there are fewer top predators than plants.
check: About ___ of energy passes to the next level.
Starting with 10,000 units, the next level gets...
There are fewer top predators because...
lessons.try: Draw an energy pyramid starting with 10,000 units of energy.

learn: Competition: organisms compete for the same resources.
Predation: one organism hunts another.
Symbiosis includes mutualism (both benefit), commensalism (one benefits, other unaffected) and parasitism (one benefits, other harmed).
check: Bees and flowers both benefiting is...
A tick on a dog is...
Organisms wanting the same food is...
lessons.try: Find an example of each symbiotic relationship.

learn: Matter cycles through ecosystems: water, carbon and nitrogen cycles.
Decomposers return nutrients to soil.
Unlike energy, matter is recycled.
lessons.try: Draw the carbon cycle including plants, animals and decomposers.

learn: Biodiversity is the variety of life in an area.
High biodiversity makes ecosystems more stable.
Threats include habitat loss, pollution and invasive species. Conservation protects habitats.
check: A major threat to biodiversity is...
lessons.try: Research an endangered species and how it is protected.
